Simultaneous determination of trace Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) by

Zhuo Guo*1, Dong-di Li1, Xian-ke Luo1, Ya-hui Li2, Qi-Nai Zhao1, Meng-meng Li1, 
Yang-ting Zhao1, Tian-shuai Sun1, Chi Ma1,

Abstract 
   The reduced graphene oxide (RGO) and Chitosan (CS) hybrid matrix 
RGO-CS were coated onto the glassy carbon electrode (GCE) surface, 
then, poly-L-lysine films (PLL) were prepared by electropolymerization 
with cyclic voltammetry (CV) method to prepare RGO-CS/PLL modified 
glassy carbon electrode (RGO-CS/PLL/GCE) for the simultaneous 
electrochemical determination of heavy metal ions Cd(II), Pb(II) and 
Cu(II).  Combining the advantageous features of RGO and CS, RGO 
and CS are used together because the positively charged CS can interact 
with the negatively changed RGO to prevent their aggregation. 
Furthermore, CS has many amino groups along its macromolecular 
chains and possessed strongly reactive with metal ions. Moreover, PLL 
modified electrodes have good stability, excellent permselectivity, more 
active sites and strong adherence to electrode surface, which enhanced 

## Page 3

  
 
2 
 
electrocatalytic activity. The RGO-CS/PLL/GCE was characterized 
voltammetrically using redox couples (Fe(CN)6
3-/4-), complemented with 
electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). Differential pulse anodic 
stripping voltammetry (DPASV) has been used for the detection of Cd(II), 
Pb(II) and Cu(II). The detection limit of RGO-CS/PLL/GCE toward 
Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) is 0.01 μg L
−1, 0.02 μg L
−1 and 0.02 μg L
−1, 
respectively. The electrochemical parameters that exert influence on 
deposition and stripping of metal ions, such as supporting electrolytes, pH 
value, deposition potential, and deposition time, were carefully studied.  
KEYWORDS: Reduced graphene oxide; Chitosan; Poly-L-lysine films; 
Simultaneous detection; Heavy metals ions 
1. INTRODUCTION 
Rapid industrialization has led to an increased discharges wastewater 
containing toxic heavy metals ions (such as Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) and 
Hg(II)), which have adverse effects on ecological environment and 
human health [1]. Although Cu(II) is essential for human health, its 
excess will cause health problems [2]. Water containing Cu(II) beyond 
the prescribed limit of 1.3 mg/L may causes lung cancer and liver damage 
in human being [3]. Pb(II), which commonly exists in industrial and 
agricultural wastewater, is severely hazardous to human beings and living 
things. Long-term drinking water containing high level of Pb(II) would 
cause serious disorders, such as kidney disease, nausea, coma, 

## Page 4

  
 
3 
 
convulsions, cancer, along with subtly negative effects on metabolism 
and intelligence [4]. Cd(II) is also utilized in many processes, including 
batteries and pigments. Its accumulation in human body causes negative 
effects such as blood pressure complications and kidney [5].  
Due to serious hazardous effects of heavy metal ions on human 
health and toxicity in the environment, it is important to develop a simple 
and highly sensitive analytical method for assessing environmental 
pollutants to improve the quality of environment and human life. Several 
methods about the detection of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II)  have been 
reported using atomic absorption spectrometry( AAS) [6-8], inductively 
coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) [9, 10], high performance 
liquid chromatography-inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry 
[11], spectrophotometry [12], X-ray absorption spectroscopy [13], 
Surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) [14]. However, most of 
the above-mentioned methods have some disadvantages, such as 
expensive, time consuming, bulky, complicate pretreatment, inconvenient 
for onsite analysis. Compared with the above methods, electrochemical 
techniques have attracted great interest in the detection of heavy metal 
ions because of their remarkable sensitivity, portability and low cost [1, 
15, 16]. The traditional mercury film electrode and hanging mercury 
electrode have good reproducibility and high sensitivity, but they have 
great risk to human health and environment. So, much attention has been 

## Page 5

  
 
4 
 
focused on how to construct high performance electrode with low toxicity. 
Differential pulse anodic stripping voltammetry (DPASV) is a simple and 
sensitive electroanalytical method for the analysis trace concentrations of 
heavy metal ions [17-19]. Moreover, a distinct advantage of ASV over 
AAS method is its ability to detect several metal ions simultaneously. So, 
the working electrode plays a critical role in the stripping analyses. An 
ideal working electrode should have multiple functions, including 
effective preconcentration, selective reaction surface and good 
repeatability.  
Graphene, which comprises two-dimensional nanostructures of  
sp2-bonded carbon atoms in a hexagonal configuration, is an excellent 
nanomaterials for electrochemistry owing to its good electrical 
conductivity, low cost, mechanical properties and high specific surface 
area [20-22]. These characteristics are propitious for facilitating electron 
transport and promoting mass transfer kinetics at the electrode surface.  
[23]. However, graphene tends to agglomerate or restack due to the strong 
π-π stacking and van der Waals interactions [24], which hinders its further 
applications. In order to conquer this problem and extend its applications, 
it is essential to modify graphene with functional materials to form hybrid 
materials with improved properties. In order to prevent the restacking of 
graphene, metal, metal oxide and conducting polymers are used to 
improve graphene distribution [24-26]. Those hybrid materials display 

## Page 6

  
 
5 
 
novel catalytic, magnetic, or optoelectronic properties.  
It is well known that chemical functionalization can tailor the 
electronic solid state properties of carbon supports, which could be 
propitious for the improvement of catalyst performance. Chitosan (CS), a 
poly (D-glucosamine), is a natural polysaccharide with primary amino 
groups in the polymer chain. Due to the outstanding properties of 
Chitosan, 
such 
as 
nontoxic, 
biocompatibility, 
hydrophilic 
and 
antibacterial activity, it has been extensively used in various fields, such 
as biomaterials [27], textile [28] , drug delivery [29] and environmental 
protection [30]. CS has been extensively investigated for several decades 
for adsorption of heavy metal ions in water treatment because of its 
excellent quality, multiple functional groups, as well as its favorable price. 
CS is regarded as a promising adsorbent because it has both amine and 
hydroxyl groups that can remove the heavy metal ions by forming stable 
metal chelates. Several investigations have shown that the RGO-CS 
hybrid systems show enhanced electrochemical properties [31-33].  
Polymer modified electrodes have been paid increasing attention in 
electrochemical analysis due to their more active sites, excellent 
permselectivity, good stability and strong adherence to electrode surface. 
Poly (L-lysine) (PLL) film can be easily formed on electrode surface by 
electropolymerization of L-lysine. PLL has been receiving much attention 
owing to its good biocompatibility, versatility and easiness of the 

## Page 7

  
 
6 
 
preparation, relatively good solubility in water, a flexible structure 
framework and a good deal of active amino groups [34, 35], which make 
them suitable for applications in electrochemical determination. 
     Recent advanced in new materials, especially the development of 
new nano-hybrid materials, have opened a new era of analytical 
techniques. By tailored functionalization and assembly, these materials 
can be easily assembled on electrode surface for the fabrication of 
sensing electrodes and the sensitive and selective detection of heavy 
metal ions [15, 36, 37]. In order to meet this requirement, the inducing of 
specific functional groups onto the electrode with the desired properties is 
particularly attractive. Combining the advantageous features of RGO and 
CS, RGO-CS nanocomposites are used together. There are plenty of 
amine groups on the CS which can strongly reactive with metal ions. In 
addition, the huge surface area of RGO makes it have a large adsorption 
capacity.  Moreover, the combination of RGO-CS with PLL can provide 
excellent electrochemical platforms for target heavy metals sensing due 
to the combinating of enlarged active surface area, strong adsorption 
capability and the specific complexing ability of the CS and PLL in 
analysis of environmental samples. To the best of our knowledge, 
RGO-CS/PLL used as sensing materials for the detection of heavy metal 
ions hasn’t been reported. Herein, we introduce RGO-CS/PLL modified 
GCE for DPASV in simultaneous determination of Cd(II), Pb(II) and 

## Page 8

  
 
7 
 
Cu(II). The detection limit (S/V=3) for Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) at this 
sensor were 0.01 μg L
−1, 0.02 μg L
−1 and 0.02 μg L
−1, respectively, which 
were lower than that of on the reported sensors for simultaneous 
determination of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II). In addition, the proposed 
sensor has been applied to simultaneous determination of Cd(II), Pb(II) 
and Cu(II) in wastewater samples with high selectivity.  
2. Experimental 
2.1 Reagents 
Natural graphite powder (320 mesh, spectrum pure), Chitosan (CS, 
deacetylation degree was about 75-85%) and L-lysine were purchased 
from Aladdin Reagent Co. (Shanghai, China). Working solutions 
containing Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) were prepared by diluting the 
corresponding standard stock solutions that were purchased from Aladdin 
(Shanghai, China). A 0.1M HAc-NaAc buffer solution (pH 4.5) was 
prepared by mixing appropriate amounts of HAc and NaAc and served as 
a supporting electrolyte during the analysis of heavy metal ions. Other 
chemical were obtained from Beijing Chemical Reagent Factory (Beijing, 
China). All of the chemicals used were analytical-regent and 
twice-distilled water was used in all experiments.  
2.2 Apparatus 
The phases of the samples were examined by powder X-ray 
diffraction (XRD) analysis using a SIEMENS D5005 diffractometer with 

## Page 9

  
 
8 
 
Cu Kα radiation at 40 Kv and 30 mA. FT-IR spectra (4000-400 cm-1) 
were recorded using a Nicolet 20 FT-IR Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher 
Scientific Int., USA) to identify the functional groups and chemical 
bonding of the prepared materials. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) 
images were obtained from FEI/Philips XL30 FEG ESEM operating at 
20.0 Kv. Differential pulse anodic stripping voltammetry (DPASV) and 
Cyclic 
voltammetry 
(CV) 
were 
performed 
in 
a 
conventional 
three-electrode cell with a Autolab-PGATA 302 electrochemical 
workstation (Metrohm). The conventional three-electrode system 
included a modified glassy carbon electrode (GCE, 3mm in diameter) as 
the working electrode, a saturated calomel reference electrode (SCE) and 
a platinum wire were used as the reference electrode and auxiliary 
electrode, respectively. DPASV was employed under optimal conditions 
and involved a preconcentration potential of -1.2 V, a preaccumulation 
time of 180 s.  After the preconcentration, the potential was held at -1.2 
V for 30 s under the static condition, followed by a positive-going DVP 
scan (with a step increment of 5 mV, amplitude of 50mV, and pulse 
period of 0.2 S) from -1.2 V to 0.2 V. Prior to the next analysis, a 
preconditioning step (60 s at 0.2 V in stirred solution) was carried out in 
order to remove residual metal ions on the surface of working electrode.  
2.3 Preparation of reduced graphene oxide-chitosan nanocomposite 
(RGO-CS) 

## Page 10

  
 
9 
 
   Graphene oxide (GO) was synthesized from graphite powder by a 
modified Hummers method [38]. The RGO-CS nanocomposites were 
prepared as follows [39]: 10 mg/mL CS solution was prepared by 
dissolving CS powder in 0.1 M pH 5.0 sodium acetate solution. 2.5 mg 
GO was dissolved in 50 mL of doubly distilled water and ultrasonicated 
for 15 min. Equal volumes of the above CS and GO solutions were mixed 
with the help of ultrasonic treatment for 5 min in a flask. And then the 
flask was put into an oil bath for reacting 10 h under 90 o C. During this 
time, the color of solution in flask was changed from yellow to black 
gradually until the GO was reduced completely. CS as reductant and 
stabilizer to transfer GO into RGO. 
2.4 Fabrication of RGO-CS/PLL/GCE   
The GCE was polished with 1.0 μm, 0.3μm, and 0.05 μm α-alumina 
powders and rinsed thoroughly with deionized water between each 
polishing step and sequentially sonicated in 1:1 HNO3, ethanol, and 
deionized water, and dried at room temperature. Six microliters (0.5 
mg/mL) of the RGO-CS nanocomposite suspension was dropped on the 
surface of GCE and dried in air. The obtained electrode was denoted as 
RGO-CS/GCE. The electropolymerization of L-lysine on RGO-CS/GCE 
was performed by dipping the above RGO-CS/GCE into PBS buffer 
solution (pH 7.5) containing 1.0 × 10−3 mol/L L-lysine by cyclic potential 
scanning from −1.0 to 0.4 V for 30 cycles with a scan rate of 100 mV s−1. 

## Page 11

  
 
10 
 
The final obtained electrode was denoted as RGO-CS/PLL/GCE. 
2.5 Procedure for electrochemical testing of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) 
DPASV was carried out in a 20 ml electrochemical cell containing 
acetate buffer (0.1 mol L−1, pH 4.5) as supporting electrolyte medium and 
the target metal ions with varying concentrations from 1.0×10-9 M to 
1.0×10-8 M. Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) were deposited at the potential of 
-1.2 V for 180 s by the reduction of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II). The anodic 
stripping (reoxidation of metals to metals ions) of the electrodeposited 
metals was performed in the potential range of -1.2 to 0.1 V. The peak 
currents at potential about -0.82 V, -0.54 V and -0.11 V vs. SCE for Cd(II), 
Pb(II) and Cu(II) were measured, respectively.

C-H stretching vibration of CS skeleton, the C-O stretching vibration of 
-NHCO- and the N-H bending NH3 [42] and the stretching vibrations of 
C-N [43], respectively. The FT-IR spectrum of GO (Fig. 2b) exhibits the 
characteristic absorptions from oxygen-containing functional groups. In 
detail, the absorption band at 3415 and 1398 cm-1 can be assigned to the 
stretching vibration and deformation vibration of O-H, respectively. The 
band at 1724 cm-1 belongs to the C=O stretching vibration of COOH 
groups, while the band at 1627 cm-1 derives from the vibration of the 
adsorbed water molecules and/or the contribution of the skeletal vibration 
of unoxidized graphitic domains. The stretching vibration peaks of C-O 
(epoxy) and C-O (alkoxy) are observed at 1200 and 1050cm-1, 
respectively [44]. As for the RGO (Fig. 2 c), the peak at 3431 cm-1 was 
attributed to O-H stretching vibration, and the peak at 1560 cm-1 could 
correspond to the O-H bending vibration and skeletal ring vibrations, the 
peak at 1088 cm-1 was due to stretching vibrations of C-O-C [45]. 
Compared with GO, the peaks of oxygen functional groups are 
disappeared or reduced for RGO, which suggests that many oxygen 
groups were removed during the transformation from GO to RGO. In

binding energy decreased significantly. According to the XPS peak area, 
the O/C ratio of graphene is 6.96%, far less than the O/C ratio of 
graphene oxide by 45.39%. This suggests that the O elements have been 
reduced successful in the graphene. Meanwhile, from N 1s spectra of 
RGO-CS (Figure 3 c), it is obviously observed that three peaks centered 
at 399.4, 400.3 and 401.5eV, which correspond to the amine (C-NH2), 
amide (C-NH-C=O) and the protonated amine species (C-N+) [47, 48]. 
The result was conformed that the CS has anchored into the RGO 
composite.

Figure 4 SEM images of CS (a), RGO (b), RGO-CS (c) and RGO-CS/PLL (d). 
    
The morphologies of CS, RGO, RGO-CS and RGO-CS/PLL were 
characterized by SEM as shown in Fig. 4. For CS (Fig. 4a), there is a 
rough surface and the internal structure is solid. It is shown in Fig. 4b that 
the RGO sheets displayed a typical wrinkled and crumpled smooth 
surface of graphene, and the sheets stacked together to form a typical 
multi-layer structure. For RGO-CS (Fig.4c), the SEM image reveals an 
entirely different surface morphology compared to the CS. It can be seen 
that CS was fully encapsulated in RGO sheets or as a spacer to inhibit of 
their aggregation. Meanwhile, some mico-wrinkled stripes protuberances 
can be found in the RGO-CS surface, which can provide the interspace to 
adsorption of the heavy metal ions. For RGO-CS/ PLL (Fig.4d), a large 
number of rod-like fibre closely attach on the surface of RGO-CS after 
the electropolymerization of PLL, indicating the formation of PLL onto 
RGO-CS sheets.  
3.2. The electropolymerization of L-lysine 
    The L-lysine polymer film modified electrode was synthesized by 
electropolymerization of L-lysine on the RGO-CS/GCE surface. The 
experiment was performed in PBS buffer solution (pH 7.5) containing 1.0 
× 10−3 mol/L L-lysine with cyclic voltammetric sweeps in the potential 
range from −1.0 to +2.0 V. As shown in Fig. 5, the cathodic peak is

## Page 20

  
 
19 
 
could be attributed to the presence of RGO film on the electrode surface 
with excellent electrical conductivity and fast electrode transfer rate. For  
RGO-CS/GCE electrode (curve c), the ΔEp increased and peak current (Ip) 
decreased, indicating that CS could block the electron transfer between 
electrode surface and [Fe(CN)6]3-/4-. That is attributed to the insulativity 
of CS. On RGO/PLL/GCE (curve d), the peak currents of redox peaks 
increased with the ΔEp value decreased, which could be attributed to 
attraction of the amino group cations of the PLL to Fe(CN)6
3 −/4− leading 
to more easily redox of of Fe(CN)6
3−/4− [49]. On RGO-CS/PLL/GCE 
(curve e), the biggest redox peak currents appeared with the smallest ΔEp 
value of 112 mV. Hydrogen bonds exist between CS and PLL. The rate of 
electron transfer is accelerated by the movement of electrons through 
hydrogen bonds between CS and PLL [50]. According to Randles-Sevcik 
equation [51], ipa= 2.69 × 105 n3/2ACD1/2 ν1/2, where ipa is the anodic peak 
current (μA), n is the number of electrons transferred, A is electroactive 
surface area (cm2), C is concentration (mol/cm3), ν is the potential 
scanning rate (mV s−1) and D is the diffusion coefficient (cm2/s). The 
electroactive surface area is 0.093, 0.086, 0.074, 0.069 and 0.052 cm2 for 
RGO-CS/PLL/GCE, RGO/PLL/GCE, RGO-CS/GCE, RGO/GCE and 
bare GCE, respectively. This indicates that the electrochemical reactivity 
of RGO-CS/PLL/GCE electrode is better than that of RGO/PLL/GCE, 
RGO-CS/GCE, RGO/GCE and bare GCE electrode. 

## Page 21

  
 
20 
 
Electrochemical impedance spectrum (EIS) is also used for 
investigation of the capability of electron transfer on the surface of 
different electrodes. In electrochemical impedance measurement, the 
semicircle diameter of impedance equals the electron transfer resistance 
(Ret), which controls the electron transfer kinetics of the redox probe at 
the electron surface. Fig. 7 is the Nyquist diagrams of bare GCE (a), 
RGO/GCE 
(b), 
RGO-CS/GCE(c), 
RGO/PLL/GCE(d) 
and 
RGO-CS/PLL/GCE (e) recorded in 1.0 mmol/L Fe(CN)6
3-/4- solution 
containing 0.5 mol/L KCl with the frequency swept from 105 to 0.1 Hz. A 
semicircle of about 341 Ω in diameter for bare (curve a) at higher 
frequencies indicates a diffusion limited step of the electrochemical 
process. After modified by RGO (curve b), the semicircle diameter was 
remarkably decreased to about 197 Ω, which showed that the presence of 
RGO could effectively accelerate the electron transfer. But, after 
modified RGO-CS nanocomposites (curve c), the semicircle diameter 
increased significantly to about 264 Ω compared with the RGO/GCE. The 
results demonstrated RGO-CS nanomaterials could increase the electron 
transfer resistance to the flow of electrons and decrease the conductivity 
of the electrode, which is consistent with the CV results above. This also 
demonstrated that RGO-CS film was successfully immobilized on the 
GCE surface. After modified by RGO/PLL and RGO-CS/PLL (curve d 
and e), the semicircle diameter was decreased to about 179 and 83 Ω. The

## Page 24

  
 
23 
 
RGO-CS/PLL/GCE is due to that larger amount of reduced metal could 
be deposited at deposition potential by the reduction of metal ions. 
RGO-CS/PLL/GCE can provide excellent electrochemical platforms for 
target heavy metals sensing due to the combinating of enlarged active 
surface area, strong adsorption capability and the specific complexing 
ability of the CS and PLL in analysis of environmental samples. These 
advantages make the RGO-CS/PLL nanocomposites be an ideal sensing 
nanomaterial 
suitable 
for 
the 
electrochemical 
detection 
or 
preconcentration of trace amounts of heavy metal ions, as illustrated by 
Scheme 1. It is known that peak response of heavy metal ion is directly 
proportional to its concentration in solution. At this stage, large amounts 
of target metal ions (Cd (II), Pb (II) and Cu (II)) can be adsorbed or 
forming a complex onto the surfaces of the nanomaterials. When the 
potential is held at deposition region, Cd (II), Pb (II) and Cu (II) will be 
reduced on the surface of the electrode and metal crystal growth occurs. 
In this way, Cd (II), Pb (II) and Cu (II) are accumulated and then stripped 
out. The more Cd (II), Pb (II) and Cu (II) are adsorbed on the surface of 
RGO-CS/PLL nanocomposite, the more it will be released, thus 
strengthening the stripping peak response. Moreover, the potentials for 
the reoxidation of Cd (II), Pb (II) and Cu (II) on RGO, RGO-CS, 
RGO/PLL are more negative than that observed on RGO-CS/PLL 
modified GCE, indicating that the reoxidation process is more favorable

at the pH 4.5. The lower pH value (3.5 and 4.0) result in a reduction peak 
current, which is possible due to the protonation of the hydrophilic groups 
reducing the absorption of metal ions[19]. The peak current at the higher 
pH value (5.0 and 5.5) decreased, which is possible due to the hydrolysis 
of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II). So, pH 4.5 was chosen as the optimal pH 
value for the analysis. 
3.5.3 Effect of deposition potential 
   Deposition potential is an important parameter for stripping 
techniques and has a significant effect on the sensitivity. The influence of 
deposition potential on the stripping response of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II)  
were studied. The deposition potential was varied between −0.9 and −1.4 
V under optimized pH condition. The results presented in Fig. 10 (b) 
indicates that the peak currents of mixed ions increase remarkably as the 
deposition potential negatively shifts from -0.9 to-1.2 V. The more 
negative the deposition potential, the more easily Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) 
were reduced, thereby causing the obvious increase of the stripping peak 
currents. Three well-separated stripping peaks corresponding to Cd(II), 
Pb(II) and Cu(II) are obtained at -1.2 V with the relative higher peak 
currents. When the deposition potential becoming more negative, the 
reproducibility of stripping currents for Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II)  
became poor, because hydrogen evolution was beginning to be significant 
in the medium at such negative potentials [19]. Furthermore, the metals

Figure 10 The effects of solution pH (a), deposition potential (b), and deposition time 
(c) on the stripping currents of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II)  at RGO-CS/PLL/GCE 
electrode in 0.1 M acetate buffer solution containing 1.0 μg L
− 1of Cd(II), Pb(II) and 
Cu(II). 
 
3.6. Electrochemical detection of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) 
   The DPASV characterization was further performed to investigate 
simultaneous determination of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II). For different 
concentrations of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) in the mixture was performed 
at the RGO-CS/PLL/GCE and experiment was investigated when 
changing the concentration of one species whereas the others were kept 
constant. Fig. 11 shows the DVASV responses of the RGO-CS/PLL/GCE 
towards Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) at different concentrations. Cd(II), Pb(II) 
and Cu(II) are detected at potentials of -0.82, -0.54 and -0.11V, 
respectively. The corresponding calibration curve from 0.05 to 10.0 
µg.L-1 were  
ip(µA)=6.91+2.51 C (µg.L-1); (0.05 to 2.0 µg.L-1, R=0.996)  (1) 
ip(µA)=8.26+0.57C (µg.L-1); (2.0 to 10.0 µg.L-1, R=0.998)  (2) 
for Cd(II),  
ip(µA)=7.01+0.4 5C(µg.L-1);  (0.05 to 2.0 µg.L-1, R=0.996)  (3) 
ip(µA)=7.41+0.09 C(µg.L-1); (2.0 to 10.0 µg.L-1, R=0.999)  (4) 
for Pb(II),  
and  
ip(µA)=7.20+0.51 C(µg.L-1);  (0.05 µg.L-1 to 2.0 µg.L-1, R=0.997) (5) 

## Page 30

  
 
29 
 
ip(µA)=7.62+0.168 C(µg.L-1); (2.0 µg.L-1 to 10.0 µg.L-1, R=0.998)  (6) 
for Cu(II), respectively. The limit of detection (LOD) (based on a 
signal-to-noise ratio of 3 (S/N = 3) were found to be 0.01 µg.L-1 for 
Cd(II), 0.02 µg.L-1 for Pb(II) and 0.02 µg.L-1 for Cu(II), respectively. 
Moreover, the limits of detection for Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) are much 
lower than the guideline values in drinking water given by the WHO (For 
Cd(II): 0.003 mg.L-1; Pb(II): 0.01 mg.L-1; Cu(II): 2.0 mg.L-1). It is clear 
that the RGO-CS/PLL electrode shows the lower limit of detection than 
most of the electrodes listed in Table 1.  
In addition, we measured the maximum adsorption capacity toward 
Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) onto RGO-CS/PLL at room temperature, as 
shown in Fig. 11d. It can be seen that the RGO-CS/PLL could adsorb 
these ions and the maximum adsorption capacity toward Cd(II), Pb(II) 
and Cu(II) is 47.14, 18.96 and 16.33 mg.g-1, respectively. This experiment 
leads to a conclusion that the sensitivity is related to the adsorption 
capacity of the materials.

3.9 Reproducibility and stability of electrode 
The repeatability and stability of the electrode could be evaluated by a 
series of repetitive experiment of DPASV. Firstly, the repeatability was 
examined by performing 10 times at the same standard solutions (5.0 μg 

## Page 35

  
 
34 
 
L
−1) Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II), the relative standard deviation were 1.7%, 
2.2% and 2.4% of each of Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II), which showing that 
the reproducibility were good. At the same time, the stability was 
examined by recorded every day over 3 weeks, the maximum deviations 
obtained were 4.2%, 3.9% and 4.4%, which showing that the composites 
has long-time stability. 
3.10 Analysis of real samples 
In order to evaluate the applicability of this method, the proposed 
electrode was used to examined the concentration of Cd(II), Pb(II) and 
Cu(II) in tap water by the standard addition method, and the same as 
above mentioned optimal conditions was used in this experiments. The 
result listed in Table 3, the recovery of Cd(II) were 96.00-103.33%, and 
the recovery of Pb(II) were 93.33-97.6%, and 96.66-101.33 of Cu(II). 
Above all, the RGO-CS/GCE/GCE can be utilized as a selective and 
precise electrode to determination metal ions, and have a better 
reproducible.

4. Conclusions 
 In this paper, a new enhanced sensing platform base on the 
RGO-CS/PLL modified GCE was established. The combination of 
RGO-CS with PLL can provide excellent electrochemical platforms for 
target heavy metals sensing due to the combinating of enlarged active 
surface area, strong adsorption capability and the specific complexing 
ability of the CS and PLL in analysis of environmental samples. This 
working electrode was used to simultaneously determination of Cd(II), 
Pb(II) and Cu(II) heavy metal ions. Three good defined and sharp 
stripping peaks can be obtained for Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II), and the 
stripping peak currents show a good linear proportionality from 0.05 
µg.L-1 to 10.0 µg.L-1 with a detection limit 0.01 µg.L-1 for Cd(II), 0.02 
µg.L-1 for Pb(II) and 0.02 µg.L-1 for Cu(II), respectively. The limits of 
detection for Cd(II), Pb(II) and Cu(II) are much lower than the guideline 
values in drinking water given by the WHO. Finally, the proposed 
electrode was successful applied to the analysis of the tap water samples.
